On Sun, 26 Aug 2001 08:18:54 GMT, Jason Bell wrote:

>Again with the laughing in your face. You would do well to explain
>how de-clumping, followed by riffle shuffling, constitutes cheating
>before you "frankly" toss about that accusation, which I take
>very seriously indeed.

The DCI Universal rules state that:

"21. Shuffle
All shuffling must be done so that the faces of the cards cannot be
seen. Regardless of the method used to shuffle, players' decks must be
sufficiently randomized."

So, if you look at your deck while you're shuffling, you're cheating.
If you pause to rebuild your deck (e.g. sideboarding) then you have to
start shuffling all over again.

Note that 3 riffle shuffles are not enough to randomise a 60-card
deck. That's even assuming that they are good riffle shuffles (which
many aren't). If 3 riffle shuffles are the norm in Canadian Magic
then that explains why folk such as you are stacking their deck prior
to the shuffles. You're all cheating because decks "must be
sufficiently randomised". You might perhaps claim that "sufficiently"
is a weasel word which would permit such cheating but I wouldn't
accept that. The idea of randomisation is that the cards are equally
likely to be in any position in the deck. It should be possible, if
unlikely, for all of one type to be together. If the
stacking/shuffling procedure is designed to prevent this then it is
not random.

I've seen someone blatantly stacking their deck prior to a perfunctory
shuffle in a VEKN event too. As long as some people think that such
deck-rigging is legitimate, the rest of us should shuffle the spots
off their cards as a matter of course. Of course, you have to watch
what players do when they are shuffling their opponents deck too. One
Magic player has just been given a 3-year suspension for stacking his
opponent's deck while shuffling it.

Andrew

More than 'three'.

VEKN 3.2:

All shuffling must be done so that the faces of the cards cannot be seen.
Regardless of the method used to shuffle, players' decks must be sufficiently

randomized. Each time players shuffle their decks (before the game or during
the game), they must present their decks to their predator for additional
shuffling and/or cutting. At the judge's discretion, players may request to
have a judge shuffle their cards rather than pass that duty to their predators.
By presenting their decks to their predators, players state that their decks
are sufficiently randomized.

After decks are presented and accepted, players who do not consider their
opponents' decks to be sufficiently randomized must notify a judge. The head
judge has final authority regarding whether a deck has been sufficiently
randomized.

Once predators have the opportunity to shuffle and/or cut players' decks, the
cards are returned to their original owners. If the predator has shuffled the
player's deck, that player may make one final cut.

--

> sufficiently randomised". You might perhaps claim that "sufficiently"
> is a weasel word which would permit such cheating but I wouldn't

Before you wade into this, with your accompanying accusations,
I first invite you to talk to any Level 3 or better Magic judge for
clarification on the rule you've cited, before you get your foot any
farther down your throat.
Next, I submit that if you present your deck for cutting without
assuring that you have re-distributed your ash heap, hand, and
cards in play from your last game into your library (or in the case
of Magic, lands, graveyard, hand, and in play), you are
in violation of the rule above. The original poster, who has had
a run of low probability outcomes (not seeing a card for half
his deck when he has 8 or more copies in the deck), is clearly in
violation of the "sufficiently randomized" rule, so is he doomed
to be called a cheater by you for this Catch-22?

> The idea of randomisation is that the cards are equally
> likely to be in any position in the deck. It should be possible, if
> unlikely, for all of one type to be together. If the
> stacking/shuffling procedure is designed to prevent this then it is
> not random.

This is only true if no shuffling occurs after the de-clumping.

LSJ, I need VEKN's official position on this before I play
a tournament game. When and under what circumstances
will I be allowed to inspect the card faces in my deck
between games? I've read VEKN 3.2, but it is unclear
whether de-clumping should be considered "shuffling"
as defined there.

No, it does not ensure a lack of clumping, it merely increases the
chance that the deck is randomized, by removing obvious ordered
card arrangements within the deck. An inspection of the card faces
can be useful to detect and dissipate obvious orderliness within
the deck (multiple cards with the same name together, a great
number of a certain card type together, repeated Torn Grapple
Undead from last game's ash heap) which was not dissipated by
regular shuffling or might not be dissipated in later shuffling.
That you shuffle afterwards allows that such cards or types have
the random chance of meeting again.
It is sensible that this is more difficult for Jyhad
players to understand, as the vampires are not distributed
within the play deck. With Magic, it is perfectly clear that 10
lands next to one another may very well not randomly distribute
with a bout of regular shuffling. I suppose Jyhad players could

other.

technique. Try 3 riffles, some overhand, 4 more riffles, then the overhand

during shuffling.

a greater number of cards, and rarely feel the full brunt of a

and shrug at Steve Bucy's experience as just bad luck,
but I know his experience well, as do several of my Magic
playing friends. It is not bad luck, it is what can happen
when you fail to ensure that your deck is randomized.

fact required by the rules.

> THIS IS NOT RANDOM.

You can shout it as often as you like, it will not make your statement
true.

properly

Yes, and given that difficulty of perfectly interleaving on a shuffle,
it makes even more sense to remove obvious orderly arrangement
of cards before or during the randomization process, lest those
orderly groups be part of the non-interleaved clumps.

Point of information, you don't want perfect interleaving anyway,
since riffle shuffling with full interleave is not a
randomization technique. Don't believe me? Take 4 cards,
and simulate a riffle shuffle twice, and you have the same order
you started with. 8 cards? three times. 90 cards? 11 times.

> Yes, I call it cheating. And yes, if I see someone doing this I'll riffle
> their deck an additional 5-6 times.

And your opponent will be happy for you to do it. More randomization
can't be bad if random is the goal. Only less random can be bad.
However, if you in addition call your opponent a cheater, he'll probably
have the same opinion of you that I do.

> manually sort them, you remove all the effects of prior shuffling, and
need

feelings about the proper number of final shuffles or when the de-clumping
excercise should happen, but I tend to do a mix of riffle and
overhand, and I tend to shuffle more than anyone else I know.

"having a bunch of extra cards in the deck that it'll probably need

to get rid of" is a straw man. It is a straw man because it creates
its own assumption that the deck in question has cards it does not
need and knows which cards those are. There is no point addressing
such an argument, as it has answered itself through its own inapt
or limiting assumptions. Of course one should dispose of those
cards or replace them with better choices.

Your scarecrow also avoids or pretends to settle part of the larger
discussion, where those extra cards were useful parts in existing
ratios or specialized cards with enormous game effects, with a better
overall chance of sifting the deck to reach the most time-appropriate
cards. The only counter I've seen to this is the ever-so-slightly
increased chance of getting particular cards or card-combos,
not enough to counter the bonus of decreased fear of running
out of cards and the opportunity of discarding critical cards when
they arrive in hand at inopportune moments.

- Jason Bell

> Does moving cards within your deck based upon whether they have the same

Irrelevant, since "shuffling" must be done without seening the face of the

If a "randomizing" process is "sufficient" (as required by the VEKN rules),
then it won't matter how clumped or not the deck is prior to the process.
The deck has the same probability of being "clumped" afterward in either
case. This is inherent in the idea of a "randomized" deck.

> regular shuffling or might not be dissipated in later shuffling.

process, then the process is not "sufficiently" random.

umpire but Magic used to have comparatively primitive rules - it was
one reason I quit the game.

>Next, I submit that if you present your deck for cutting without

>cards in play from your last game into your library (or in the case
>of Magic, lands, graveyard, hand, and in play), you are

You do this by shuffling. You may not look at the cards while you're
shuffling.

>The original poster, who has had
>a run of low probability outcomes (not seeing a card for half
>his deck when he has 8 or more copies in the deck), is clearly in
>violation of the "sufficiently randomized" rule, so is he doomed
>to be called a cheater by you for this Catch-22?

A run of low probability outcomes is not proof of cheating - quite the
opposite in this case. Players don't want their cards to be clumped
so clumping is a sign that players are not cheating. Instead, to call
someone a cheat, you need to catch them manipulating the cards, e.g.
by stacking their deck.

>> The idea of randomisation is that the cards are equally
>> likely to be in any position in the deck. It should be possible, if
>> unlikely, for all of one type to be together. If the
>> stacking/shuffling procedure is designed to prevent this then it is
>> not random.
>

break those card arrangements before further attempting
to randomize the entire deck.

Messages.Author: Sam Hillier
Messages.Body:
Jason Bell wrote :

>So I inspect the deck for
>evidence of order that I can easily detect, and attempt to
>break those card arrangements before further attempting
>to randomize the entire deck.
>

You're making another simple mistake here, Jason. When you go through your deck to eliminate clumps of, say, Master cards, you are removing randomization.

By "inspecting the deck for evidence of order that you can easily detect", you are destroying randomization. Randomization does not imply that the master cards must be equally distributed throughout the deck. If your deck ends up clumped after you perform a good, quality shuffle (without looking at the faces), that doesn't mean that the randomization was poor.

Now, at the completion of a game it is certainly a good idea to go manipulate your deck, to ensure that your permanents aren't clumped. This is a sensible thing, but it is not randomizing the deck. After doing this, and before proceeding to the next game, you must then sufficiently shuffle your deck. Pausing in the middle of this to look at the faces and de-clump again, in the name of "randomization" is wrong. The very nature of randomization says you can't manipulate the order of the deck.

Which leads to the one other confusion I see. You mistake two definition of "order". One is the way in which the cards themselves are organized in an enumerated list. The other is some subjective idea that order must consist of equally distributed masters, combat cards, reactions, etc. The first definition is the one involved in randomization; randomization is meant to ensure that no artificial order is present in the deck; i.e. that means that you don't get to set this order yourself. The second is completely divorced from randomization, seeking this type of order is cheating.

> of his deck. Repeated low probability outcomes provides evidence
> that the player is in violation of that rule.

from www.m-w.com:

Main Entry: random
Function: adjective
Date: 1565
2b: being or relating to a set or to an element of a set each of whose
elements has equal probability of occurrence <a random sample>

The set in question is all the possible arrangements of the cards in your
deck, from all-clumped to all-separate. "sufficiently shuffled" is
supposed to select one arrangement from that set at random.

Let's take an extremely simple example. Suppose I have a deck of six
cards, three of which are Minion Tap, two of which are Fifth Tradition, and
one of which is Lost in Crowds. A truly random shuffle would ensure that
the deck order of:

{MT, MT, MT, 5th, 5th, Lost}

...would be equally as likely to occur as:

{MT, 5th, Lost, MT, 5th, MT}

One is totally clumped, one is totally non-clumped. BOTH should be equally
likely. If you use ANY method to give yourself a greater chance of having
a non-clumped deck, then your shuffle is not random. It's that simple.

If you have shuffled sufficiently (facedown pile shuffle, plus many riffle
shuffles/overhands), and your deck STILL turns up clumped, congratulations;
you have just proven why "random" means "random". It's supposed to be
possible for this to happen.

Herein lies the beauty ;)
Several arguments about good/bad cards end up in if the card in question is
a multipurpose card. These are generally considered to be GOOD. Now,
most designers seem to consider only those cards that are explicitly having
two distinctly different effects as multipurpose, but several other cards
that have only one effect can be played for good usage in several
situations. People don't refer to these as multipurpose, only accept that
they (almost) never jam your hand.
Any card that can be used in (almost) any situation is a multipurpose
card, and they also tend to be support-cards. You decide what you want to
do, pick those cards, and then you add support-cards to help you doing
it. I'll happily say that Majesty is a multipurpose card (until I'm stuck
with an Immortal Grapple or Thoughts Betrayed *grin*) as it either
leaves me with a bonus blocker/bouncer or gives me an additional action.

So I try to build a deck counting how many card-consuming actions or
reactions I'll probably do during a game (that I win), and then I add the
support-cards. Admittedly I start out deciding the D-rating I'll be able
to handle and inflict.

I couldn't find anything giving "irregular". 1a's 'lacking a pattern'

duplicates form a pattern, which must be removed. But NO duplicates is
also a pattern, and ensuring that by sorting faceup also breaks the
definition, not to mention breaking the definition of "at random", since
you have used a definite method.

Pile shuffling face down is an indefinite method because you can't see the
faces of the cards, and have no idea where you're sorting them and into
what piles. I can agree with Jason's assertion that you need to ensure
that you achieve separation of cards that were played during the last game,
as otherwise you have a non-random, RECOGNIZABLE situation; pile shuffling
once, facedown, with 7 or more piles will ensure this. 6+ riffle shuffles
afterwards will then return the deck to a near-completely random state;
whether that state then includes large numbers of adjacent cards or not is
irrelevant.

What I have stated is that *if* the "clumps" present at the start of
a "randomizing" process are preserved by that process, then the process

Try this: I hand you a deck of 52-playing cards that I tell you is

you either don't believe me when I tell you that the deck is
randomized or you don't know how probability works.

Note that nowhere in the above experiment does the state of the deck
before I "randomized" it come into the picture.

10 riffle shuffles is about right, IMO. Proving this is non-trivial.
See a good general survey of the topic which I copy below.

Note that the results mentioned are based upon theoretical models of
shuffling rather than physical experiments with real people and cards.
And that the studies to date have mainly looked at standard 52-card
decks of playing cards. Extending results from these to Vampire is
non-trivial because:

a) Vampire decks usually have more than 52 cards. Apart from
theoretical considerations, riffle-shuffling a 90-card deck is
physically difficult and unlikely to be done well, especially if it's
in sleeves.

b) Vampire decks usually contain many identical copies of the same
card.

Andrew

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
From http://www.sciencenews.org/20001021/mathtrek.asp

Disorder in the Deck
by Ivars Peterson

Card players sometimes get lazy, shuffling a deck fewer times than
necessary to randomize the cards. Indeed, persistently sloppy
shuffling can have a significant impact on play—an effect that experts
(and gamblers) can exploit to their advantage.

About 30 years ago, tournament bridge players started using
computer-shuffled rather than hand-shuffled decks. Almost immediately,
there was an outcry protesting the apparently wild fluctuations in the
distribution of cards of different suits in computer-dealt hands.

However, the problem lay not in the computer but with human
expectations. Subsequent research showed that hands in which suits are
evenly distributed, that is, hands with four cards of one suit and
three of each of the other suits, are actually more common in games in
which people do the shuffling than they should be according to theory.

The reason for such a pattern is that cards during bridge play tend to
clump together in groups of four of the same suit. Careless shuffling
doesn't do enough to break up the groups, and when the cards are dealt
out, the four players get a fairly even distribution of suits.

In fact, before the advent of computer shuffling, the intuition of
bridge players had been shaped by generations of improperly shuffled
cards. A close look at books published in the past reveals that some
experts had figured out that cards generally aren't shuffled well and
had developed strategies that took such quirks into account. When
computer shuffling was introduced, many of these strategies had to be
revised.

How many times must a deck of 52 cards be shuffled before the cards
are randomly distributed? It turns out that trying to answer this
question raises a number of subtle issues concerning both card
shuffling and various measures of randomness.

In the May 1986 American Mathematical Monthly, statisticians David
Aldous of the University of California, Berkeley, and Persi Diaconis
of Stanford University argued that roughly seven riffle shuffles are
sufficient to achieve an acceptable degree of disorder in a deck of 52
cards. (In a riffle shuffle, the deck is cut into two, possibly
unequal packets, and the two packets are then raggedly interleaved.)
Diaconis and David Bayer of Columbia University later refined this
result.

With five or fewer shuffles, the original order of the standard deck
is strongly in evidence. With more than seven shuffles, the original
order has virtually disappeared. So, although no finite number of
shuffles will ever make anything completely random, it doesn't take
long to get close enough for practical purposes.

Such abrupt transitions from order to randomness show up in a variety
of mixing processes. You might ponder the same sort of behavior in
your own kitchen when stirring together white flour and cinnamon. At
first, you see thick streaks as the ingredients mingle. After a few
more strokes, the whole mixtures suddenly smooths to a tan color.

Whether as many as seven shuffles are really necessary, however,
depends on how you define and measure randomness, say Nick Trefethen
of the University of Oxford in England and Lloyd Trefethen of Tufts
University in Medford, Mass. They now argue in the Proceedings of the
Royal Society that five shuffles would do a reasonable job of
randomization and six would make it practically certain the cards are
thoroughly mixed.

To determine how many shuffles would adequately randomize a deck,
Diaconis and Bayer worked with a statistical measure known as the
"total variation norm." This number quantifies the rate at which an
ideal gambler could expect to make money, on average, if allowed to
place bets against a fair house by taking advantage of any residual
pattern among cards in a deck. In this model, the "total variation
distance to randomness" falls below 0.5 after seven shuffles.

The Trefethens adopted an alternative definition of randomness—one
rooted in the telecommunications industry. They considered a deck of
cards as a packet of information.

If you know the location of every card in the deck, you have all the
necessary information about the deck. If the deck is then shuffled
until it is truly random, you end up with zero information about the
card distribution. For the Trefethens, the issue was how quickly
shuffling destroys information about the card distribution.

Technically, the researchers looked at a number that "quantifies the
rate at which an infinitely competent coder could expect to transmit
information, on average in the limit of infinitely long message
lengths, if permitted to encode signals arbitrarily in shuffled decks
of cards."

Using computer simulations of riffle shuffles, the Trefethens found
that, according to their measure of the information left about the
card distribution, the amount of information (degree of order)
decreases steadily with each shuffle, reaching virtually zero
information with the sixth shuffle and staying there with each
subsequent shuffle.

"It is not obvious, even to experts, what the full significance is of
the distinction between our two measures of randomness," the
researchers conclude. Which measure of randomization is relevant for
card players may even depend on the types of games they play.

What should be clear, however, to the everyday player is that, no
matter which model is relevant, just three lackadaisical shuffles
isn't enough.

References:

Aldous, D., and P. Diaconis. 1986. Shuffling cards and stopping times.
American Mathematical Monthly 93(May):333.

Ball, P. 2000. Shuffling: What's the deal? Nature Science Update (Oct.
4). Available at http://helix.nature.com/nsu/001005/001005-8.html.

Bayer, D., and P. Diaconis. 1992. Trailing the dovetail shuffle to its
lair. Annals of Applied Probability 2:294.

Berger, P. 1973. On the distribution of hand patterns in bridge:
Man-dealt versus computer-dealt. Canadian Journal of Statistics 1:261.

Diaconis, P. 1996. The cutoff phenomenon in finite Markov chains.
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 93(February):1659.

Folger, T. 1991. Shuffling into hyperspace. Discover (January):66.

Keller, J.B. 1995. How many shuffles to mix a deck? SIAM Review
37(March):88.

Kolata, G. 1990. In shuffling cards, 7 is winning number. New York
Times (Jan. 9).

______. 1985. Prestidigitator of digits. Science 85 6(April):67.

Peterson, I. 1990. Islands of Truth: A Mathematical Mystery Cruise.
New York: W.H. Freeman.

______. 1984. Mathematical shuffling. Science News 125(March 31):202.

randomize a deck of cards? Proceedings of the Royal Society, London A

http://www.pubs.royalsoc.ac.uk/proc_maths/abstracts/2002.htm.

This thread started as a tangent to the "smaller deck" thread. Steve Bucy
posted that after his tremendously painful recent experiences with
variance, that he will be trying out the short-deck idea as a possible
cure, as the math DOES support it.

Jason Bell responded, opining that the flaw was probably just in Steve's
shuffling, not his deck size. He suggested shuffling in a different
fashion to reduce variance, and his details were:

"Table shuffle into 7 stacks between EVERY game, then
riffle, then overhand, then riffle some more. Sometime during
all that, go through the deck face up and separate repeated
cards."

The predictable hullaballoo has resulted directly from "go through the deck
face up" part, and the "separate repeated cards" part.

The first objection I have is to ANYONE going through their deck face up.
If you do this, you need to shuffle a WHOLE lot (7+ times would satisfy me)
to ensure that you are unable to retain any information gained from looking
at your deck. A tangent to this objection has been the number of shuffles
after the face-up separation; Jason's words on this were "once assured that
the de-clumping was followed by 3 or more riffle shuffles", indicating that
he considers 3 to be the minimum amount required.

However, 3 is noticeably insufficient; if I were inclined to cheat, I would
sort my deck out into a perfect order while pretending to 'de-clump', then
approach the table, perform three rapid, perfunctory riffle-shuffles, and
then hand my deck to my predator to cut, answering any objections with "Ah,
but I DID shuffle it three times." It is not difficult to see that many
cards that were sorted out will NOT be separated by only three shuffles,
due to the difficulty of properly riffling a 90-card deck. Not only that,
I know what "key cards" to look for that will predict my next few cards,
because I just saw my deck face-up. This is bad.

The second objection is to the opinion itself. Separating cards that are
identical is a form of deck-stacking, as is the method you describe of
inserting your Masters in between every 5th minion card. You are
absolutely correct in your statement that if you shuffle your deck
sufficiently, this will be no more or less random than shuffling a
completely sorted deck. However, if we accept the truth of your statement,
clearly Steve's shuffling CANNOT be at fault for his clumping, and we must
look elsewhere.

The only way Jason's opinion can ever be valid is if he fails to shuffle
properly, such that his manually-separated and stacked cards do not ever
have a chance of reforming into clumps. This is in violation of the VEKN
Rules, which is where all of us have chimed in.

> and shuffling? After sorting out my masters and inserting them, if I
> follow VEKN shuffling rules, and present my deck to my predator whats
> the problem..or is there a problem and you guys are talking about
> something else?

If the sorting method results in any detectable advantage, clearly you have
not followed VEKN shuffling rules, as you have contraverted the
randomization effect of shuffling.

> people trying to qualify something as more/less random? Or just get
> better shuffling rules instated?(ie you have to shuffle 10 times
> before a game?)

The shuffling rules as they are now are satisfactory, since they allow a
player's predator to shuffle what he/she considers to be an insufficiently
shuffled deck. I fully intend to start taking advantage of this, and I
invite all of my future predators to shuffle my deck as much as they
desire; *I* do not fear the random factor, as every additional shuffle
simply increases the "randomness".

your
> deck to eliminate clumps of, say, Master cards, you are removing
randomization.

I disagree with this. The goal of the de-clumping is to remove predictable
sorting that resulted from the organization of the play order of cards.
If you often find that your equipment, retainers, and discipline masters
often occur in large groups, this is less likely one of the variables of
shuffling,
and more likely related to how you grab all your cards together between
games. Once that sort of order is broken, I have no objection to
that order or any other that is imposed by the act of shuffling. But
if, after some nominal shuffles after bringing my deck back into one,
I find 4 or 5 instances of Torn/Grapple/Undead, it doesn't take a
statistician to predict that this is the result of play order sorting,
not some random outcome.

I think the largest simple mistake being made on this thread is
the presumption by players about the extent to which their
shuffling regimes are actually randomizing their decks.

> Which leads to the one other confusion I see. You mistake two definition
> of "order". One is the way in which the cards themselves are organized in
an
> enumerated list. The other is some subjective idea that order must
consist
> of equally distributed masters, combat cards, reactions, etc. The first
> definition is the one involved in randomization; randomization is meant to
ensure
> that no artificial order is present in the deck; i.e. that means that you
don't get
> to set this order yourself. The second is completely divorced from
randomization,
> seeking this type of order is cheating.

I strongly disagree with this. While you are of course correct that
unevenly
distributed card types are perfectly consistent with randomization, what
you miss is the case where many repeated games demonstrate highly uneven
distribution, as the original poster suggested was his experience (and
of which I have ample experience in Magic). This sort of uneven
distribution, of the same character, in repeated games, is evidence
of incomplete randomization. That further shuffling is in order
after obvious order is broken obviates your characterization of
cheating.

- Jason Bell

If your shuffling is sufficiently random, there is no predictable
sorting. That's the whole point. You could get, quite literally, any
order. Perfectly acceptable orders for random shuffling would be all
your master cards, all your action modifiers, all you actions, all your

What this is all tending to suggest is that:

- once you've played a game, you're tending to end up with small batches
of master, actions, action modifiers etc. (This happens to many
of us)

- these then go back into the deck, roughly in those groups

- when you're shuffling, your shuffling isn't thorough enough to
randomly re-assign these cards to places in the deck, instead
keeping those lumps in parts

"LSJ" <vte...@white-wolf.com> wrote

> Try this: I hand you a deck of 52-playing cards that I tell you is
> randomized. Then I ask you to inspect the top card. You find the Ace
> of Spades. I then ask you: what is the probability that the next
> card (the one under the Ace of Spades) is the 2 of Spades?
>
> If your answer is anything other than "1 in 51", then that means
> you either don't believe me when I tell you that the deck is
> randomized or you don't know how probability works.

What if I found the AS, followed by 2S, 3S, and 4S?
What if I knew that the deck was sorted numerically
by suit before shuffling began, because you had just
won a game of Solitaire.
Would that be evidence that your deck is not sufficiently
randomized?

By separating those cards before completing the shuffling process,
you may still not have a perfectly randomized deck, but the lack of
randomization is less likely to have its own predictable order that
can affect the progress of the game (as the A234 sort would affect
a game of Spades or Hearts). If I can't have random, I prefer
unpredictable to predictable.

When I advise de-clumping of obvious order, I acknowledge
that randomization is not a perfect process, and where it
is done imperfectly, it should not have a predictable outcome.
I advised Bucy to do so because he described a situation
that I recognized from my own difficulties in randomizing
Magic decks.

I have come to hypothesize that the shuffle-resistant
clumping in Deckmaster games comes from uneven handling of
the cards. Some cards are quickly laid upon the table and
left there, others are moved quickly to the discard pile,
while others spend a great deal of time in the player's hand.
The different handling of the cards leads to different wear
or different levels of oil and dirt that can cause some cards
to slightly stick together, resisting the casual riffle shuffle.
This also corresponds to the experience Bucy described where
his problem developed over time, perhaps as his cards began
to wear.
Therefore, for Bucy, I advised visual inspection for clumping
as well as separating the cards into piles on the table by
placing them into multiple different stacks one card at a time,
in addition to a regular shuffling regime.

- Jason Bell

I've just spent an entertaining hour reading the archives of
DCIJUDGE-L on the Wizards site. There was an extensive discussion of
this matter earlier this year, in which such matters as the legality
of "mana-weaving" was discussed (note that that it was explicitly

repealed). There was an interesting technical claim made in support

which I preferred. There was no clear consensus on the matter and a
fair amount of frustration that there was no official authority to
resolve it.

The last word went to a newly-appointed netrep for the list and his
post is copied below. It's fairly anodyne, IMO, and doesn't really
resolve the issues raised. However note that he says, "If you think
the player is intentionally ordering his deck with the intent of
gaining game advantage this is cheating". That's precisely what
you're doing, Jason, isn't it? Like it or not, that makes you a cheat
in the eyes of this most senior of DCI judges.

Overall, I find it very amusing that, after all this time, the DCI has
made little progress in defining such a basic matter as how decks
should be shuffled. I always thought that it was an incompetent
organisation and am even more convinced of it now. The VEKN has
little to learn from them and should have the courage to write its own
tournament rules now rather than copying theirs.

Andrew

<DCIJU...@ORACLE.WIZARDS.COM>
From: Michael Feuell <e...@CROCKER.COM>
Subject: NR Re: Shuffling and "Statistics"
Content-Type: text/plain; charset="iso-8859-1"

> But instead of reading dozens of emails about that, I'd rather hear some
> OFFICIAL guidelines about what is punishable and how to
> detect/correct/penalize it. That's one of the goals of this list, isn't it?

Insufficient randomisation falls into two cases:

1) insufficient shuffling, this is when a player takes a deck in any
known configuration and then fails to shuffle it sufficiently.
2) insufficiently random, this is when a deck is in an ordered manner.

note: it is possible to take a deck, shuffle it a 'sufficient' number
of times and still end up with a deck that by chance is in an ordered
manner.

From the Penalty Guidelines:

Procedural Error-Major
A Major Procedural Error occurs when a player performs an
unintentional, disruptive action at the tournament.
(C) A player does not sufficiently randomize her deck before
presenting it to her opponent.

The penalty is a warning.

This of course can be upgraded based upon multiple offences.

If you think the player is intentionally ordering his deck with the
intent of gaining game advantage this is cheating and warrent s a DQ
without a prize. These of course are the guidelines, as a judge it is
up to you to best weigh the situation at hand and the appropriate
penalty.

You don't want to let players get away with gaining an advantage their
opponent does not have intentionally or not. Yet you also don't want
to be so pedantic that you start counting the number of riffle
shuffles. The floor rules now suggest that a player shuffle an
opponents deck. As a judge you should encourage your players to do
this. Players will be less likely to invest time in ordering their
deck if their opponent always shuffles it.

-Michael

The probability of drawing 45 cards from a 90 card deck and drawing no
instances of a subset of 8 cards:

(90-8)! * (90-45)!
pr(!A) = ------------------ = 0.278%
90! * (90-8-45)!

The two trials are independent (given sufficient randomization between
them), thus the total probability would be pr(!A)^2 = 7.7 x 10^-4
percent. Very small.

Note 1: This is true for _any_ subset of 8 cards; there will always
be a set of 8 cards, in every game, that will satisfy this criterion.
How many different sets of 8 cards are you monitoring per game?

Note 2: If you play 100 games, the chance of not having pr(!A) occur
is:

1 - ((1-pr(!A))^100) = 24.3%

Which is just to note the fact that the more games one plays, the more
likely one is to see all sorts of improbable behaviors, due to the
nature of randomness.

> Then try blaming it on the vagueries of random outcomes.

I'm not sure what else one could blame it on, after the fact?
Probability can only give you likelihoods for each possible outcome.
Approaching the limit of large numbers of games, the statistics of
your sample should converge to the predicted probabilities; if not,
then perhaps you can come to some conclusions about the bias of your
shuffling, goo on your cards, or chimerstry usage by your opponents.
But two games doth not a significant sample make.

Hope that helps,
Alex

Hi
In a game we had a couple of days ago, I borrowed a deck from another
player. A gangrel deck Basilia-oriented with 6 Basilia in a crypt of
12. The first 5 vamp i controlled weren't Basilia! (1/132 probability
of that situation happening). The player who borrowed me the deck was
my predator and very happy to see from the other side the only game
(probably) with that deck absolutely useless.

If you want a sufficently random shuffle try this:
Equip yourself with a complete set of dices;
1) prepare d8+1 stacks
2) on each stack put d4 cards until you've completely stacked your
deck
3) use appropriate die to select a first and a second stack to stack
togheter
4) riffle d6 times
5)add another stack selected as in 3)
6)repeat 4) and 5) until you have again the complete deck
7)riffle the whole deck d10+1 times
8)pass your deck to your predator
9)stand up, do three turns around the table,clockwise in an odd day,
counterclockwise in an even day
10) take the deck of your pray and repeat steps 1-10 until you have
again your deck
11) let your predator cut the deck
12) start to play

Otherwise do not lose time stacking, de-coupling etc. just riffle a
lot and have fun with the draw you got.
(BTW i got a VP retreating after i exahusted my cards with the
probably-but-not-surely-basilia deck)

Anyone ever tried to play a series of games without shuffling
in-between? Probably you need different deck-building!?!
